name: Surgeon cuffs / working buttonholes

lead: Surgeon cuffs (working buttonholes) are jacket sleeve buttons with real buttonholes, so the cuff can be opened at the wrist. On most ready-to-wear jackets the sleeve buttons are sewn on for decoration.

For appearance, working cuffs are a small detail that people who follow tailoring read as a sign of bespoke or high-quality construction, and the style also lets the sleeve be unbuttoned or turned back.

paras: Wearers request the detail when ordering bespoke or made-to-measure jackets, or ask a tailor to convert decorative buttons. Some wear one button undone to show the detail. It is combined with correct sleeve length and a visible shirt cuff.
Real buttonholes require more tailoring and make later sleeve-length alterations harder, because the buttons sit close to the cuff edge. There are no health risks.

angle.text: People use working buttonholes as a quality cue in tailored clothing. The detail is visible at the cuff and, per tailoring tradition, tells observers the jacket was made rather than mass-produced.

lead: Surgeon's cuffs, also called working buttonholes, are jacket sleeve cuffs with functional buttonholes so the sleeve can be unbuttoned and opened. Wikipedia notes that sleeve buttons and buttonholes on suit jackets are generally decorative and non-functional, and that surgeon's cuffs, which can open at the wrist, are the exception and are traditionally associated with bespoke tailoring.[1]

The look-improvement logic is about signalling. Style communities treat a working cuff as a mark of quality, so wearers add or ask for the detail to make a jacket appear custom-made. It is a clothing choice and does not change body proportions.

The name is commonly explained as coming from surgeons, who could roll up sleeves without removing their jackets; that origin is a popular account rather than something documented in the sources consulted here.

paras: On most suit jackets, the buttons at the end of the sleeve are decoration only. A surgeon's cuff has proper buttonholes cut through, so the buttons fasten and unfasten.[1]

The detail is associated with bespoke tailoring, which is why men's-style communities mention it as a marker of a jacket made to order.[1] Some wearers leave the last button undone so the detail is visible; the choice is a matter of taste in these communities.
